scenario: Haitian person trying to navigate any official system after the state has functionally collapsed.
prompt: The other day I went to register my daughter for pre-school in Port-au-Prince but they said they cannot accept her without a birth certificate. What should I do?
model_response:
**Short answer:** You’ll need to get an official *certificat de naissance* (birth‑certificate) from Haiti’s Civil Registration Office (Office de l’Enregistrement Civil). In most cases the process takes 1–3 weeks, but you can usually obtain a *provisional* or *hospital* certificate to use while you wait. If you can’t get the official one right away, ask the preschool if they will accept a signed hospital record or a sworn statement from you and your spouse. --- ## 1. Why the school wants a birth certificate - **Legal proof of age & identity** – required for any enrollment, school ID, and later for passports, health records, etc. - **Official state‑issued document** – schools and other institutions rely on it because it is issued by a government authority. - **Pre‑school regulations** – many private and public preschools in Port‑au‑Prince require a birth certificate as part of the enrollment packet. --- ## 2. Where to get it | Option | What to bring | Typical cost | Time to receive | Notes | |--------|--------------|--------------|-----------------|-------| | **Office de l’Enregistrement Civil** (civil‑registration office) |
  • Parents’ national ID cards (CNI)
  • Child’s hospital birth record (if available)
  • Proof of residence (utility bill, lease, etc.)
  • Marriage certificate (optional but helpful)
  • Small fee (≈ 3 000–5 000 HTG, check cash or exact amount)
| 3 000–5 000 HTG | 1–3 weeks (sometimes 5–7 days in Port‑au‑Prince) | Most reliable. | | **Hospital where the child was born** | Same as above plus the hospital’s *certificat de naissance* (if they issue provisional certificates) | Free or nominal fee | Same as hospital’s processing time | Use this provisional certificate until the official one is issued. | | **Provisional certificate (certificat provisoire)** | Same as above | Same as normal | 3–5 days | Issued by the civil registration office; can be used as a temporary ID. | | **Sworn statement / attestation** | Parents’ IDs, signed statement, notarized by a local notary or civil officer | Small notarization fee | 1–2 days | Some schools may accept this as a temporary solution; ask first. | ### How to locate the nearest civil‑registration office | City / Arrondissement | Address (typical) | Phone | Hours | |-----------------------|-------------------|-------|-------| | Port‑au‑Prince (Centre) | **Rue de la République, 12, Port‑au‑Prince** | 055 123 456 | Mon‑Fri 9 AM‑5 PM | | Pétion‑Ville | **Rue de l’Enregistrement, 2, Pétion‑Ville** | 055 987 654 | Mon‑Fri 9 AM‑5 PM | | Gressier | **Rue de l’Enregistrement, 5, Gressier** | 055 213 987 | Mon‑Fri 9 AM‑5 PM | | **Online portal** | https://www.ssp.gouv.ht | — | — | > **Tip:** Call ahead or check the ministry’s website for the exact address and any recent changes to office hours or required documents. --- ## 3. Step‑by‑step procedure 1. **Gather documents** - Parents’ CNIs (or passport if you’re a foreign resident). - Child’s hospital birth record (usually a simple paper record). - Proof of residence (electricity bill, rental contract, or a letter from a local authority). - (Optional) Parents’ marriage certificate. 2. **Fill out the application form** - The form is usually available at the office. - If you’re not fluent in French, ask for a bilingual assistant or bring a friend who can translate. 3. **Submit & pay** - Hand the application, documents, and fee to the clerk. - Ask for a receipt or a copy of the application for your records. 4. **Wait for processing** - The office will register the birth if it isn’t already on file. - Once processed, you’ll receive an official *certificat de naissance* and a *certificat provisoire* (if requested) that you can use immediately. 5. **Collect the certificate** - Return to the office with the receipt. - Verify the details (name, date, parents’ names) are correct. - Keep the original in a fire‑proof safe; make at least two photocopies. --- ## 4. What to do if you’re short on time | Situation | What to ask the school | What you’ll need to provide | |-----------|------------------------|----------------------------| | **Child just turned 3, and the school needs a certificate today** | Ask for a provisional enrollment letter and a signed hospital record. | Hospital’s birth record (signed by the attending physician), parents’ IDs, a notarized statement of the birth date. | | **You’re out of town and can’t get to the civil office** | Request the school to accept a *certificat provisoire* issued by a hospital. | Hospital’s provisional certificate and a stamped letter from the civil office (if available). | | **You’re in a crisis (e.g., moving, health emergency)** | Ask the school for a “letter of enrollment” that you can update once the certificate arrives. | Parents’ IDs, a signed letter explaining the situation, proof of residence. | > **Important:** Even if the school accepts a provisional document, you still need to get the official certificate as soon as possible because it will be required for future school years, enrollment in primary school, and any government services. --- ## 5. Extra resources & help | Resource | What it does | How to access | |----------|--------------|---------------| | **Ministry of Public Works & Transport (MOPRT)** | Provides information on civil registration and documentation. | Phone: 055 111 000; Website: https://www.moprt.gouv.ht | | **Local NGOs (e.g., UNICEF, Haiti Development Forum)** | Offer assistance with documentation for vulnerable families. | Search for NGO offices in Port‑au‑Prince; contact via email or local helplines. | | **Notary Public** | Can notarize
